title: The twelve links
hookLine: ignorance, formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the senses, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, aging-and-death (SN 12.1)

lines: A PAINTED WHEEL BY THE DOOR.
cards: Near the entrance of a Tibetan temple, you may find a huge painted wheel held in the claws and teeth of a fierce figure. Around its outer rim run twelve small pictures. A blind person with a stick.
A potter at his wheel. A monkey swinging through a tree. People in a boat.
A house with windows. A couple embracing. A man with an arrow in his eye.
Someone drinking. Someone picking fruit. A pregnant woman.

teach.b: The very first sutta in the book on dependent arising, in the Connected Discourses, lays the chain out. With ignorance as condition, there are formations.

Then the links run on: consciousness; name-and-form, the mind and body together; the six senses; contact, where a sense meets its object; feeling, pleasant, painful or neither; craving; clinging; becoming; birth; and finally aging and death, with sorrow, grief and despair.
Such, the sutta says, is the arising of this whole mass of dukkha. Now match them to the wheel.

teach.h: THE BLIND ONE, THE POTTER, THE MONKEY.
teach.b: Ignorance is the blind person, feeling the way. Formations, the potter, the way past actions shape what comes. Consciousness, the monkey jumping from branch to branch.
Name-and-form, the people in the boat, traveling together. The six senses, the house with its windows. Contact, the embrace.
Feeling, the arrow in the eye. Craving is drinking, clinging is grabbing fruit, becoming is the pregnancy, then birth, then the body carried off.
The paintings are a later Indian and Tibetan tradition; the suttas give only the list.

The same sutta then runs the chain again as an ending: with the ending of ignorance, formations end, and so on, link by link, to the ending of this whole mass of dukkha. Buddhists read the chain in more than one way.
The Theravada commentaries spread it across three lifetimes: past, present and future.

teach.h: ACROSS LIVES, OR IN A MOMENT.
teach.b: Some teachers also read it moment by moment, in a single afternoon.
Both readings are part of the living tradition.

how: In Tibetan monasteries the wheel of life is often painted near the entrance with the twelve links around its rim; in Theravada lands the links are chanted and studied, often following the commentaries' three-life reading.

o: a cause of good luck in the next life
a link in the chain of dependent arising
a painted wheel by a temple door

games.q: you're looking at the wheel of life. you spot a monkey swinging from branch to branch. which link is it?
games.why: the monkey is consciousness, jumping from one object to the next; craving is someone drinking, clinging is grabbing fruit.

practice: On each breath, name one link and let its picture appear: ignorance, the blind one; formations, the potter; consciousness, the monkey; name-and-form, the boat; six senses, the house; contact, the embrace; feeling, the arrow; craving, drinking; clinging, grabbing fruit; becoming, the pregnancy; birth; aging and death.
Then go around again, slower. If you lose your place, start at the blind one.

wordCard.voice: Nidana. A link in the chain of dependent arising: from ignorance to aging and death, each one leaning on the one before, and each one able to end.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit nidāna: a cause or source, the usual word for each of the twelve links.

carryVoice: Your line: twelve links. A puzzle on a temple wall, and a teaching. That's day three hundred forty-nine.
